findings.title: Authorization bypass via client-controlled flag using global_access
findings.body: `enable_advanced` grants advanced pagination (which allows negative offsets, bypassing normal result boundaries) to any user with `is_superuser` or `organization_context.member.has_global_access`. `has_global_access` is a broad flag not necessarily tied to audit log read permissions, and combined with the client-controlled `optimized_pagination=true` query param, this allows a wider set of users than intended to trigger a different, less-tested code path that manipulates raw SQL slicing (negative offsets). This is a privilege-escalation-adjacent risk: a feature flag toggled entirely by request parameters controls which pagination/query logic runs, with no audit or rate limiting around it.

findings.title: Negative offset slicing produces invalid/undefined SQL querysets
findings.body: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset`. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing/slicing (unlike Python lists) and will raise `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported` or similar errors. This will crash the endpoint rather than provide any 'efficient reverse pagination', directly contradicting the claimed functionality and causing 500 errors whenever a negative offset cursor is supplied (which is also client-controlled via the cursor cookie/param).

findings.title: Dead/misleading advanced-features code with no real optimization
findings.body: The class docstring and comments claim 'negative offset support', 'streamlined boundary condition handling', and 'optimized query path for large datasets', but the actual implementation is nearly identical to BasePaginator.get_result except for the broken negative-offset branch. There is no genuine performance optimization (e.g., no index-based seek optimization, no changed query plan) despite the PR title and description promising enhanced pagination performance. This is misleading to future maintainers and reviewers evaluating the actual behavior change.

findings.title: Incorrect extra-row trimming when negative offset branch taken
findings.body: The trimming logic `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra` uses the original (pre-negative-offset) `offset` variable, but when the negative-offset branch is used, `start_offset` differs from `offset`. This inconsistency means the extra-row removal check can be wrong, causing an extra row to leak into cursor results or a valid row to be dropped, depending on the sign/magnitude of the offset the queryset lookup actually used.

findings.title: No tests added for new optimized pagination branch
findings.body: The PR introduces an entirely new code path (`OptimizedCursorPaginator` with `enable_advanced_features`) gated by a request parameter and permission check, but no test files are included in the diff. Given the branch changes query semantics (negative offsets) and gates access by permission, there should be tests covering: unauthorized access attempts, negative offset cursors, and equivalence with the standard paginator for typical cases.

findings.title: Comment describes unimplemented feature in Cursor class
findings.body: The added comment claims `self.offset = int(offset)` 'enables efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets' via negative offsets, but `Cursor` itself does no bounds checking and the actual consumer (`OptimizedCursorPaginator`) mishandles negative offsets (crashes on Django querysets). The comment overstates functionality that is broken elsewhere in the PR, which is confusing for maintainers trying to understand supported Cursor semantics.
